content.text: The diagram shows an object, P, undergoing uniform circular motion. Which arrow shows the direction of the net force acting on P?

content.alt_text: A circle showing the path of object P, a tangent arrow at P labelled 'Direction of motion', and four candidate arrows W, X, Y and Z radiating from P.

content.text: W
X
Y
Z

For P the speed is constant but the direction of the velocity is constantly changing, so the net force cannot be along the direction of motion. Consider $\Delta v$ between two nearby points on the path.

For uniform circular motion $\Delta v$ over a short time is always at right angles to the velocity, and it points in the same direction relative to the path at every point. Use that to locate the centre.
C

P travels around the circle at constant speed, so the magnitude of its velocity is unchanged while its direction changes continuously. A change of momentum requires a net force, and that force always acts along $\Delta v$. Over a short interval $\Delta v$ is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, so the net force is perpendicular to the direction of motion: it is the centripetal force, directed along the radius towards the centre of the circle.

In the figure P sits on the left-hand side of the circle, so the centre lies to the right of P. Of the four arrows, W points away from the centre (opposite to the net force) while X and Z are tangential to the path; only Y points from P towards the centre. The net force is therefore in the direction of arrow Y, option C.

items: 1 mark: identifies the net force as the centripetal force directed towards the centre of the circle (arrow Y)

content.text: Which of the following provides evidence for the wave model of light proposed by Huygens?
Emission spectra
Diffraction of light
Black body radiation
The photoelectric effect
Huygens' wave model predicts that a wave spreads into the region behind an obstacle and spreads out on passing through a narrow gap. Which of the listed effects tests that prediction?
Also check which of the options is explained by Planck and Einstein's quantum model rather than by any wave model.
B

Huygens' wave model treats light as a wave, so it must bend and spread as it passes an edge or a narrow gap, and it must interfere where two beams overlap. The evidence is therefore any effect in which light spreads rather than travelling in straight lines.
Examine each option:

items: A - Emission spectra: a hot low-density gas emits only certain discrete wavelengths. A continuous wave model cannot produce line spectra; Planck and Einstein explained them with photons.
C - Black body radiation: the distribution of energy across wavelengths from a heated body. The classical wave model failed to predict it and Planck's quantum hypothesis was needed instead.

D - The photoelectric effect: electrons are released only above a threshold frequency, and their maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency but not on the intensity. Photon theory explains this, not a continuous wave.

B - Diffraction of light: light spreads into the geometric shadow behind an obstacle and through a gap, producing bright and dark fringes whose spacing widens as the opening narrows. This is a wave-only behaviour.

content.text: Diffraction is the effect that the wave model predicts and that a particle or ray model cannot produce, so the correct option is B.

items: 1 mark: identifies diffraction, the spreading of light around obstacles and through gaps, as evidence for the wave model of light

content.text: Which of the following is a fundamental particle in the Standard Model of matter?
Hadron
Neutron
Photon
Proton

The Standard Model is built from a small set of elementary particles together with the forces between them. Take each option in turn and ask whether it is assembled from smaller constituents or is as small as matter gets.
C

A fundamental particle is one that cannot be broken down into smaller constituents. The Standard Model treats matter as six quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom) and six leptons (electron, muon, tau and the three neutrinos), and treats the photon, the $W$ and $Z$ bosons and the gluons as the carriers of the four interactions.
Test each option:

items: A - Hadron: a collective name for particles (protons, neutrons, pions) built from quarks, so it is composite.
B - Neutron: a baryon made of one up quark and two down quarks, so it is composite.
C - Photon: the force carrier of the electromagnetic interaction, with no internal structure at all, so it is elementary.
D - Proton: a baryon made of two up quarks and one down quark, so it is composite.

content.text: Only the photon is a fundamental particle, so the correct option is C.

content.text: For continuous rotation the torque must keep turning the coil in the same rotational sense. Ask what has to happen to the current in the coil when it reaches the half-turn position.

Compare the two ring arrangements: a split-ring commutator must be divided along a plane that contains the axis of rotation, so that each half stays in contact with its own brush. Then match the type of supply the reversing arrangement requires.
D
For the coil to keep turning in one direction, the current in it must reverse every half rotation, so that the torque produced by the motor effect always acts in the same rotational sense.

That reversal is the job of a split-ring commutator: the ring is divided into two halves by a cut along a line that contains the axle, so each half keeps contact with its own brush and, after a half turn, the two halves have swapped brushes. In D the two halves lie either side of the axle, so each brush rests on a half-ring and the circuit is complete. In A and B the two halves lie above and below the axle, which puts each brush in one of the insulating gaps, so the circuit is open.

The supply must also be DC. With an AC supply (A and C) the current reverses at the supply frequency as well as at the commutator, so the torque alternates and the coil cannot sustain rotation in one direction.
Only D pairs a DC supply with a correctly oriented split-ring commutator, so the correct option is D.

content.text: The photoelectric effect is mathematically modelled by the following relationship:
In this model, the symbol $\phi$ represents the amount of energy
supplied by a photon to an electron.
retained by an electron after being hit.
required to release an electron from a material.
left over after a collision of a photon with an electron.
Read the equation in words: maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron = energy carried by the incident photon minus something. Identify what that 'something' must represent.

Since $K_{\max} = 0$ at the threshold frequency, the term must be the energy barrier that the electron has to overcome just to leave the surface, and it can depend only on the material, not on the light.
C

Read the equation in words: the maximum kinetic energy of the fastest photoelectron is what is left of the photon's energy $E = hf$ after the electron has paid an energy barrier to get out of the metal.

That barrier can be identified from the threshold condition. Below the threshold frequency $f_{0}$ no electrons are emitted at all, and exactly at $f_{0}$ they escape with $K_{max} = 0$, so the photon energy there exactly equals the barrier:

$\phi$ is therefore the work function of the metal: the minimum energy needed to release an electron from the surface. It is a property of the metal alone, so it does not vary with the frequency or the intensity of the light.

items: A is wrong: the energy the photon supplies to the electron is $hf$, not $\phi$.
B is wrong: an electron cannot retain energy from a collision in which it was never released, and the energy it does keep is $K_{max}$, not the barrier.
D is wrong: the energy left over after the interaction is $K_{max} = hf - \phi$, which is the remainder, not the part removed.

content.text: So $\phi$ is the energy required to release an electron from a material, which is option C.

items: 1 mark: identifies $\phi$ as the work function, the minimum energy required to release an electron from the metal surface

content.text: For a charge in the rod the magnetic force is $F = qvB\sin\theta$. As the rod rotates about P, the velocity of Q stays in the plane of the page, so the angle between that velocity and $B$ does not change. What does that do to the size of the force, and to the component of that force along the rod?

Because the rod's own length vector rotates through exactly the same angle as the force direction, the product of the two does not change sign or size during the revolution. Sketch the emf against time on that basis and compare it with the four graphs.
D

The rod is pivoted at P, so every charge carrier in it travels on a circle about P with speed $v = \omega r$, where $r$ is the distance of the carrier from P. That velocity is tangential to the circle and therefore always perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, which is directed into the page, so the magnetic force on each carrier, $F = qvB$, has the constant magnitude $q\omega rB$ and acts along $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$. For a tangential $\mathbf{v}$ and a field into the page, that force is radial, i.e. along the rod itself.

The rod's length vector turns through exactly the same angle as the force direction, so the product never changes sign, and it never changes size either, because $B$, $\omega$ and $L$ are all constant. The emf between P and Q is therefore the same at every point of the revolution: it is never zero and it never reverses.

The sinusoidal graphs A and B are what a rotating closed coil produces, because the flux through a closed loop changes sinusoidally; the flux rule cannot be used here, since a single rod encloses no area. C is wrong because the carriers never move parallel to $\mathbf{B}$. content.text: The diagram shows a type of particle accelerator called a cyclotron. Cyclotrons accelerate charged particles, following the path as shown.

content.alt_text: Cross-section of a cyclotron: two D-shaped dees separated by a gap, an alternating voltage across the gap, magnets above and below, a particle path spiralling outward from the centre to a target.

content.text:
An electric field acts on a charged particle as it moves between the gap between the dees.
A strong magnetic field is also in place.

Once a charged particle has the required velocity, it exits the accelerator towards the target.

Which of the following is true about a charged particle in a cyclotron
It increases speed while inside the dees.
It only accelerates while between the dees.
It undergoes acceleration inside and between the dees.
It slows down inside the dees and speeds up between the dees.
Inside a dee there is no electric field, only the magnetic field. What does a magnetic field do to the speed of a moving charge, and what does it do to the direction of its velocity?
Now consider the gap between the dees, where the alternating electric field acts. Which region changes the particle's speed, and does the word 'acceleration' require the speed to change?
C

Inside a dee the electric field is zero, so the only force on the charged particle is the magnetic force $F = qvB$, which is always perpendicular to the velocity. A magnetic force does no work, so the particle's speed is unchanged there, but its velocity is continually being turned, so the particle is accelerating (centripetal acceleration) inside the dees. That is exactly why the path drawn on the diagram is a widening spiral rather than a circle.

Between the dees the particle crosses the gap in the electric field of the alternating voltage. Here the force is along the particle's motion, so this is where its speed increases, and the alternating voltage reverses sign every half cycle so the particle is always pushed forwards. The particle is therefore accelerating both inside and between the dees.

Option A fails because the speed does not change inside the dees; option B fails because the direction of the velocity does change inside the dees; option D fails because nothing inside the dees slows the particle down. Option C is the only statement that is true in both regions.

content.text: Fix the reference case first. The magnet's N pole faces coil X and moves towards it, so the field through X points away from the magnet and is increasing. Lenz's law says the induced current opposes that increase: which pole must the face of X nearest the magnet become?

For each option, use the right-hand grip rule on the arrow in the changing coil to find the direction of the field inside that coil, and remember that on the axis outside a coil that field points the same way on both sides of it. Then ask whether the flux through X is increasing or decreasing, and in which direction.
Compare the direction in which each option drives the field inside X with the direction the approaching magnet requires. Only one option matches on both the winding sense and the change in flux.
D

Reference case: the magnet's N pole is the pole facing X and the arrow shows the magnet moving towards X. Field lines leave that N pole, so the flux through X points to the right and is increasing. By Lenz's law the induced current must oppose that increase, so it drives the field inside X from right to left, making the left-hand end of X a north pole that repels the approaching pole.

content.latex: \Phi_X \to \text{increasing to the right}\;\Rightarrow\; B_{X} \to \text{right to left}

content.text: Now use the same test on each option. On the axis outside a coil, the field points in the same direction as the field inside that coil, on either side of it, so the changing coil's arrow and winding sense fix the direction of the flux it threads through X, and the words increasing or decreasing fix how that flux is changing.

items: A: the changing coil is to the left of X, its current is increasing and its field inside the coil points to the left, so the leftward flux through X is increasing and the induced current in X drives the field to the right, making X's left-hand end a south pole. Opposite to what is needed.

B: compared with A both the winding sense and the arrow have been reversed, so the field inside the changing coil still points to the left; X is again to its right and the current is increasing, giving the same wrong direction in X.

C: the changing coil is to the right of X, its current is decreasing and its field inside the coil points to the right, so the rightward flux through X is decreasing and the induced current in X drives the field to the right, again making X's left-hand end a south pole. Wrong direction.

D: the changing coil is to the right of X, its current is decreasing and its field inside the coil points to the left, so the leftward flux through X is decreasing and the induced current in X drives the field from right to left, making X's left-hand end a north pole. This is the same current direction as for the approaching magnet.

content.text: Only D reproduces the current in X that the approaching N pole induces, so D is the correct option.

content.text: In a vacuum chamber there is a uniform electric field and a uniform magnetic field. A proton having a velocity, $v$, enters the chamber. Its velocity remains unchanged as it travels through the chamber. A second proton having a velocity, $2v$, in the same direction as the first proton, then enters the chamber at the same point as the first proton. In the chamber, the acceleration of the second proton
is zero.
is constant in magnitude and direction.
changes in both magnitude and direction.
is constant in magnitude, but not direction.
The first proton travels straight through, so the electric and magnetic forces on it must be exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Write that balance down.

For the second proton compare $qvB$ with that same $qE$, then think about what happens to the angle between its velocity and $B$ once it starts to be deflected, and therefore to the size and direction of the net force.
C

The second proton at $2v$ experiences a magnetic force $F = qvB\sin\theta$ that is twice as large as the electric force, so it is deflected. As its velocity changes, the angle between $v$ and $B$ changes and the magnetic force changes, so both the magnitude and direction of the acceleration vary.

content.text: Muons are unstable particles produced when cosmic rays strike atoms high in the atmosphere. The muons travel downward, perpendicular to Earth's surface, at almost the speed of light. Classical physics predicts that these muons will decay before they have time to reach Earth's surface.
Explain qualitatively why these muons can reach Earth's surface, regardless of whether their motion is considered from either the muon's frame of reference or the Earth's frame of reference.
The question insists on both frames of reference, so organise the answer as two parallel paragraphs and use a different relativistic effect in each.
In the muon's own frame the muon is at rest, so its own half-life is unchanged and the only quantity available to change is the distance it has to cross through the atmosphere.

In the Earth's frame the thickness of the atmosphere is unchanged, so the only quantity available to change is the muon's half-life. State which effect applies in each frame, and explain why the muon never notices its own clock slowing down.

In the muon's frame of reference the distance through the atmosphere is length contracted, so the muons only have to travel a shorter distance and can reach the ground within their short half-life. In the Earth's frame of reference the muons' half-life is time dilated, so the muons survive much longer than expected in Earth's frame and more of them reach the ground.

In the muon's reference frame, the distance travelled is less than that observed by a stationary observer on Earth's surface, due to the effects of length contraction. This shortened distance means that they will get further than would be expected by an observer observing the rest length. From the Earth's frame of reference, the time dilation means that the half-life of the muon is dilated compared to the half-life measured in the rest frame of the muon. This greater time allows more muons to reach the ground than would otherwise be expected.

content.text: Show that the vertical displacement of the electron beam at the end of the parallel plates is approximately $8.1\,\mathrm{mm}$.

content.text: When the switch is turned on, the current in rod A is greater than the current in rod B. Consider this statement. Position 2 results from the larger current in rod A, causing a larger force to act on rod B. Evaluate this statement with reference to relevant physics principles.
Write down the expression for the force between two parallel current-carrying conductors, $F = \mu_0 I_1 I_2 l/(2\pi r)$, and notice that it is symmetric in the two currents.
The rods interact only through this magnetic force, so apply Newton's third law: what does it say about the force on A compared with the force on B?

Both rods start from rest and move for the same time $t$ under forces of the same magnitude. If the forces cannot explain the difference in displacement, use $a = F/m$ and $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$ to work out what else must be different.

The statement is incorrect: the forces on the two rods are equal and opposite (Newton's third law) and $F \propto I_1 I_2$, so the larger current in A does not produce a larger force on B. Rod B's larger displacement must be due to its smaller mass, giving it a larger acceleration and hence a larger displacement in the same time.

Rod B does have a larger displacement from the original position than rod A. However this is not due to the current in rod A being larger. The force on rod B due to the electromagnetic force from rod A is the same magnitude as the force on rod A due to the electromagnetic force from rod B, according to Newton's third law. The magnitude of the electromagnetic force between both rods is given by $F = \mu_0 I_1 I_2 l/(2\pi r)$. Since the larger displacement of rod B cannot be explained by a larger electromagnetic force acting on it, it must be due to rod B having a smaller mass. A smaller mass would mean that it has a larger acceleration ($a = F/m$), causing it to have a larger displacement during time $t$.

content.text: Explain the effect on all of the forces acting on the object if the period of the cylinder's rotation is halved. Ignore the effects of friction.
List every force acting on the block before deciding what changes: its weight downwards, the reaction from the floor upwards, and a horizontal contact force from the side wall of the cylinder.

Only the horizontal force does anything to the motion. Express it in terms of the period using $F_C = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{4m\pi^{2}r}{T^{2}}$, then ask what a factor of two change in $T$ does to it.
For the other two forces, argue from the fact that the block has no vertical acceleration, so the vertical forces must still balance each other exactly as they did before.

The forces are the gravitational force downwards, the force from the floor upwards and the centripetal force from the side of the cylinder towards the centre. Since $F_C = 4m\pi^2r/T^{2}$, halving the period increases the centripetal force by a factor of 4. The gravitational force and the upward force of the floor remain unchanged because the period does not affect them.
The forces acting on the object are gravitational force downwards, force from the floor upwards and centripetal force from the side of the cylinder towards the centre of the cylinder.

Therefore, halving the period will increase the centripetal force by a factor of 4. The gravitational force downward and the force of the floor upward remain unchanged because the changing period does not affect gravitational or the vertical reaction force.

content.text: Compare the maximum height reached by the projectile, using each model. In your answer, describe the energy changes of the projectile.
Both models describe the same launch, so the initial kinetic energy is identical and the comparison has to be made through the gravitational potential energy gained per metre of height.

For the flat surface, ask whether the gravitational field strength changes at all as the object rises. For the curved Earth, remember that the field strength at a distance $r$ from the centre is $GM/r^{2}$, so it falls as the object climbs away from the surface.

The model in which the potential energy rises more slowly with height is the one in which the object travels further before its kinetic energy is used up, so state which model gives the greater height and justify it from the energy changes rather than from a formula for the height.

In both models the initial kinetic energy is the same and at the maximum height the initial kinetic energy is fully converted to gravitational potential energy. In Model A, for each metre moved vertically the same amount of kinetic energy is converted to gravitational potential energy. In Model B, because the gravitational field strength decreases with height, the amount of kinetic energy converted to gravitational potential energy per metre decreases as the object travels upward. Therefore, in Model B the object reaches a greater maximum height before all of its kinetic energy is converted to potential energy.

content.text: Many scientists have performed experiments to explore the interaction of light and matter. Analyse how evidence from at least THREE such experiments has contributed to our understanding of physics.

Pick experiments where the data were surprising enough to force a change of theory: black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect, atomic line spectra, polarisation, diffraction and interference, or the lifetime of muons. Any three are acceptable.

The verb in the question is analyse, so each example needs the whole chain: what was observed $\rightarrow$ what the accepted model could not explain $\rightarrow$ what new understanding resulted. A list of experiment names on its own will not score well.

Any three of: black body radiation experiments leading to the development of quantum physics (the shape of the black-body curve could not be explained classically and led to quantised energy $E = hf$); photoelectric experiments leading to the quantum model of light ($K_{max} = hf - \phi$ confirmed photons carry discrete energy); spectroscopy experiments leading to astrophysics and the development of the atomic model (unique line spectra identified elements and the redshift of galaxies showed an expanding universe); polarisation experiments leading to the wave nature of light; interference and diffraction experiments leading to the wave model of light; cosmic gamma ray experiments leading to the theory of special relativity and/or the Standard Model.

Three experiments on the interaction of light and matter in which the evidence changed physics. (Other experiments, such as polarisation, diffraction and interference, or muon lifetimes, are equally acceptable.)
Experiment 1: black-body radiation.

items: Evidence: the intensity–wavelength curve measured for a hot cavity did not match the curve predicted by classical theory, which diverged catastrophically at short wavelengths (the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'), and the discrepancy did not go away when the temperature or the cavity size was changed.
Limitation: classical physics could not account for the observed curve at all.

Understanding gained: energy is exchanged in discrete amounts $E = hf$ rather than continuously. Planck's quantum hypothesis, and with it quantum physics, was introduced; the quantum of light, the photon, followed, and the whole of atomic and nuclear physics rests on it.

content.text: Experiment 2: the photoelectric effect.

items: Evidence: electrons were emitted from a metal only when the frequency exceeded a threshold value that was different for each metal; emission was instantaneous even at very low intensity; increasing the intensity increased the photocurrent but did not increase the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, $K_{max} = hf - \phi$.
Limitation: a wave model cannot explain a threshold frequency, nor why the energy of individual electrons is unaffected by intensity, since a wave spreads its energy over the whole wavefront.

Understanding gained: light behaves as particles. Each photon carries a fixed energy $E = hf$ which is transferred to a single electron, so intensity sets only how many electrons are emitted, not how energetic they are. This is direct experimental evidence for the quantum model of light.

content.text: Experiment 3: atomic line spectra (the Balmer series for hydrogen).

items: Evidence: each element produced its own unique pattern of emission lines, and the four visible lines of hydrogen fitted $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ exactly, with $n_f = 2$ and $n_i = 3, 4, 5, 6$.
Limitation: classical theory, in which the electron radiates continuously as it orbits and loses energy, predicts a continuous spectrum and cannot produce sharp, quantised frequencies.

Understanding gained: electrons occupy discrete stationary energy levels and a photon of energy $E_p = hf = E_f - E_i$ is emitted or absorbed on each transition. This gave the energy level model of the atom and let the composition of stars be determined from their spectra, founding astrophysics.

content.text: In each case the evidence did more than add a detail: it removed a model and replaced it with one that could account for the data, which is why these experiments underpin the wave and quantum models of light used today.

content.text: A magnet is swinging as a pendulum. Close below it is an aluminium (non-ferromagnetic) can. The can is free to spin around a fixed axis as shown.

content.alt_text: A bar magnet swinging above an aluminium can, with the magnet's S pole to the left and N pole to the right, above the marked centre of the can.

content.text: Analyse the motion and energy transformations of both the can and the magnet.

The can is aluminium, so it is a conductor. Ask what is changing as the magnet swings towards and then away from it: the magnetic flux through the aluminium is changing, even though no battery or supply is connected to the can.

Lenz's law fixes the direction of the induced current and of the magnetic force it produces, and therefore which way the can must turn. The same law also requires that the magnet's own motion is opposed.
Close the energy account: say where the gravitational potential energy of the magnet ends up once the swinging has died away.

As the magnet swings from a high position towards the can it loses gravitational potential energy and gains kinetic energy. The magnet's motion provides a changing magnetic flux through the aluminium can, inducing an emf according to $\varepsilon = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$. This emf gives rise to eddy currents in the can, which produce resistive heating and a magnetic field that opposes the movement of the magnet according to Lenz's law. The interaction of the two magnetic fields also results in the can rotating clockwise initially. Over time this dampens the magnet's movement, and the can rotates backwards and forwards with diminishing amplitude, until the total energy is converted to heat in the can.

As the magnet swings from a high position towards the can, it loses gravitational potential energy and gains kinetic energy. The motion of the magnet provides changing magnetic flux through the aluminium can. This change in flux is greatest when the relative motion of the magnet and can is greatest, and induces an emf according to $\varepsilon = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$. This emf gives rise to eddy currents in the can, which produces resistive heating as well as a magnetic field that opposes the movement of the magnet, according to Lenz's law. The interaction of the magnetic fields of the magnet and the can, due to eddy currents, also results in the can rotating clockwise initially. Over time, this results in a dampening of the magnet's movement, and the interaction of the eddy currents' magnetic field with the magnet results in the rotation of the can backwards and forwards, with diminishing amplitude as the total energy is ultimately converted to heat. Answers could include reference to a non-uniform, clockwise rotation of the can.
